source_text: Ostendit autem inter haec veritas, quia, etsi prodesset effusa generaliter medicina motibus atque mortalibus, illis quoque, qui eam nullo studio nec ulla intentione meruissent, non tamen continuo noceret culpa nascentibus, qui nihil ad eam assensionis admovere potuissent. Ac per hoc, etsi aequalis esset gratiae peccatique taxatio, clarebat tamen ne tum quidem eiusmodi appensionem eo usque constare, ut quisquam nasci probaretur reus.
pass_a_gloss: But among these things the truth has shown that, even if a medicine poured out generally would profit motions and mortals, even those who had deserved it by no zeal nor by any intention, nevertheless a fault would not continuously harm those being born, who could have moved no assent toward it. And through this, even if the taxation of grace and of sin were equal, it was nevertheless clear that not even then would a weighing of this kind stand so far that anyone would be proved to be born a defendant.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS nascor; Blaise infants in the original-sin debate

pass_b_english: But amid these points, truth has shown that even if medicine, poured out universally, benefited bodily movements and mortal people, including those who had earned it by no effort or intention, guilt would not therefore harm newborn children who could have contributed no assent to it. Consequently, even if grace and sin were rated equally, it was clear that even then such a weighing would not extend so far as to prove anyone born guilty.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
In this book Julian usually means the Savior's gift abounding against Adam's sin (Rom 5), not later system-grace as a substance, and not 'favoritism' unless a suum-cuique definition is in play.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
